Stepwise Reducer Behavior

Stepwise Reducer enables policy-driven pipeline control immediately after the Reducer stage produces a reduced candidate value. Engineer-supplied Stepwise Reducer functions observe the current committed state alongside the reduced candidate value and explicitly decide whether pipeline execution should continue, block, or clear.

Stepwise Reducer Contract Summary

  • Stepwise Reducer functions must be pure and side-effect free
  • The pipeline provides Stepwise Reducer functions with isolated, read-only snapshots of both the current state and the reduced candidate value; these values must not be mutated
  • Stepwise Reducer functions do not return a value — they must emit exactly one decision: continue, block, or clear
  • Exactly one Stepwise Reducer function may be registered for the Reducer stage
  • Errors thrown during stepwise evaluation propagate as Vault errors and terminate the current update.

The Stepwise contract guarantees that policy evaluation is deterministic and authoritative. If a stepwise function throws an error, that error is promoted to a Vault error and immediately terminates the current pipeline execution. The in-flight candidate value is discarded, no decision is applied, and no snapshot is emitted. This ensures that policy failures never result in ambiguous control flow or inconsistent pipeline outcomes. For details on how referential isolation is enforced at every stage boundary, see Pipeline Isolation.

Stepwise Reducer participates exclusively in policy evaluation. It does not derive values, does not mutate state, and does not emit snapshots. Its sole responsibility is to determine whether the reduced candidate should be accepted, suppressed, or used to clear existing state.

Note

Because Stepwise Reducer does not return a value, failing to invoke a decision method (continue, block, or clear) leaves the pipeline awaiting a response that never arrives. This creates a policy deadlock and prevents the FeatureCell from processing further updates.

Stepwise Reducer Stage

The Stepwise Reducer stage executes immediately after the Reducer stage has produced a reduced candidate value and before that value is admitted into downstream pipeline stages.

Stepwise Reducer functions are invoked with isolated, read-only snapshots of the current committed state and the reduced candidate value, along with a decision controller. Based on this evaluation, the function must explicitly select exactly one execution outcome:

  • continue() — allow the candidate value to proceed through the pipeline
  • block() — suppress the candidate update while leaving existing state unchanged
  • clear() — clear the current committed state and terminate processing for this update

Stepwise Reducer functions must always emit exactly one decision. Failure to do so results in pipeline termination to preserve deterministic and safe execution semantics.

Diagrams
Available Stepwise Reducer Behaviors

Stepwise Reducer is implemented as a core policy behavior. Engineers supply stepwise callback functions that are executed by the core behavior during pipeline evaluation.

Core Stepwise Reducer Behavior
Behavior Description
withStepwiseReducerBehavior

stage: Stepwise Reducer

type: policy

 Executes an engineer-supplied stepwise reducer function immediately after the Reducer stage has produced a reduced candidate value. The function evaluates pipeline state and emits a control decision that determines whether execution continues, is suppressed, or is cleared.
  • Does not mutate state
  • Does not derive or return values
  • Maps decisions to Vault-native control signals
StepwiseFunction<T>
Signature Description
StepwiseFunction<T>

inputs:

  • current: T | undefined
  • candidate: T
  • decisions: StepwiseBehaviorDecisionShape

returns: void

 A policy-only function that observes both the current committed state (if any) and the newly reduced candidate value. The function must imperatively emit exactly one control decision using the provided decision controller. It does not return a value.
StepwiseBehaviorDecisionShape
Decision Pipeline Effect
continue()

type: () => void

 Allows pipeline execution to proceed normally. The candidate value continues through persistence.
block()

type: () => void

 Suppresses the current update (VAULT_NOOP). No state changes occur, but the pipeline remains active for future updates.
clear()

type: () => void

 Clears the current state (VAULT_CLEAR_STATE) and terminates processing for the current update. Subsequent updates may proceed normally.
Registering the Stepwise Reducer Behavior

The Stepwise Reducer Behavior is attached structurally when the FeatureCell is defined. This determines that the FeatureCell participates in stepwise-based post-reducer execution control at runtime.

Registering the behavior does not configure the behavior by itself. It enables the behavior so that post-reducer stepwise function supplied later via the fluent API can be applied during pipeline execution.

Note

Registering the behavior does not register the Stepwise controller. The Stepwise controller must be attached structurally when the FeatureCell is defined. 

{{`// app.config.ts

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideVault({ logLevel: 'off' }),

    provideFeatureCell(
      EmployeeService
      {  
        key: 'employees',
        initialState: [],
      },
      [
        withStepwiseReducerBehavior, 
        // Optional add-on behaviors
      ],
      [
        // Attach the Stepwise Controller structurally
        withStepwiseController
      ]
    )
  ]
};

@FeatureCell`}}<Employee[][]>{{`('employees')
@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {
  private readonly vault = injectVault`}}<Employee[][]>{{`(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Apply one or more reducers during initialization
    this.vault
      .withStepwiseReducer({
        stepwiseCallback: (current, candidate, decisions) => { 
          // evaluate current and/or candidate 
          // and return a decision
        }
      })
    ).initialize()
  }
}`}}
 
{{`export const employeeCell = FeatureCell`}}<Employee[]>{{`(
  {
    key: 'employees',
    initialState: [],
  },
  [
    withStepwiseReducerBehavior
    // Optional add-on behaviors
  ],
  [
    // Attach the Stepwise Controller structurally
    withStepwiseController
  ]
);

employeeCell
  .withStepwiseReducer({
    stepwiseCallback: (current, candidate, decisions) => { 
      // evaluate current and/or candidate 
      // and return a decision
    }
  })
  .initialize();`}}
Stepwise Reducer Function Patterns

Stepwise Reducer functions are supplied by engineers and executed by the core Stepwise Reducer behavior. While JavaScript permits many ways to express a function, only a limited set of patterns are appropriate for deterministic, policy-driven pipeline control.

Category A: Pure / Context-Free Functions (Recommended)

Pure Stepwise Reducer functions depend only on their inputs and emit deterministic decisions. They do not reference instance state and do not close over mutable external variables.

Example 1: Pure Stepwise Reducer Function

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.withStepwiseReducer({
  stepwiseCallback: (current, candidate, decisions) => {
    if (!candidate.length) {
      decisions.block();
    } else {
      decisions.continue();
    }
  }
}).initialize();
// Updates with an empty candidate value are suppressed `}}

Example 2: Factory-Generated Pure Stepwise Reducer Function

{{`// Factory produces a pure, parameterized stepwise policy
export function enforceMinimumEmployees(minCount: number) {
  return (current, candidate, decisions) => {
    if (candidate.length < minCount) {
      decisions.block();
    } else {
      decisions.continue();
    }
  };
}
// Updates with fewer than 3 employees are suppressed`}}

Category B: Instance-Aware but Correctly Bound Functions (Acceptable)

Stepwise Reducer functions may reference instance state when correctly bound. These functions remain deterministic per FeatureCell instance and must not be shared across cells.

Example 3: Arrow Function Using Instance State

{{`readonly minEmployees = 3;

readonly stepwiseCheck = (current, candidate, decisions) => {
  if (candidate.length < this.minEmployees) {
    decisions.block();
  } else {
    decisions.continue();
  }
};`}}

Example 4: Bound Instance Method

{{`public enforceActiveEmployees(
  current,
  candidate,
  decisions
) {
  const hasInactive = candidate.some(e => e.status !== 'Active');

  if (hasInactive) {
    decisions.clear();
  } else {
    decisions.continue();
  }
}`}}

Category C: Inline Lambda Functions (Allowed, Use Sparingly)

Inline lambdas are allowed but should be limited to trivial, self-contained rules. Complex inline logic can obscure intent and reduce testability.

Example 5: Inline Stepwise Reducer Function

{{`vault.withStepwiseReducer({
  stepwiseCallback: (current, candidate, decisions) => {
    // Inline lambdas make it easy to accidentally embed policy logic
    // that would be clearer as a named function
    if (candidate.some(e => e.status === 'Suspended')) {
      decisions.clear();
      return;
    }

    decisions.continue();
  }
}).initialize();`}}
Stepwise Reducer Function Anti-Patterns

Category D: External Mutable State or Missing Decisions (Discouraged)

Stepwise Reducer functions are decision-only policy hooks. They must be fully deterministic and must always emit exactly one control decision. Functions that depend on external mutable state or fail to issue a decision violate the Stepwise Reducer contract and result in invalid pipeline behavior.

Note

Because Stepwise Reducer does not return a value, failing to invoke a decision method (continue, block, or clear) leaves the pipeline awaiting a response that never arrives. This creates a policy deadlock and prevents the FeatureCell from processing further updates.

Example 6: Invalid — Missing Decision (Deadlock)

{{`vault.withStepwiseReducer({
  stepwiseCallback: (current, candidate, decisions) => {
    if (candidate.length > 5) {
      // ❌ forgot to call decisions.continue()
      return;
    }
  }
}).initialize();

// ❌ Pipeline error: Stepwise Reducer function did not emit a decision`}}

Example 7: Invalid — External Mutable State

{{`let threshold = 5;

vault.withStepwiseReducer({
  stepwiseCallback: (current, candidate, decisions) => {
    if (candidate.length > threshold) {
      decisions.continue();
    } else {
      decisions.block();
    }
  }
}).initialize();

// ❌ Behavior depends on external mutable state`}}
Stepwise Reducer Function Summary

Stepwise Reducer Function Comparison

The following table summarizes the practical differences between the Stepwise Reducer function styles demonstrated above. While all valid examples may execute correctly, they differ in determinism, policy safety, and long-term maintainability.

Summary Rule

Any Stepwise Reducer function must be deterministic, must operate only on the provided snapshots, and must emit exactly one decision. Functions that rely on external mutable state or fail to issue a decision introduce nondeterminism or deadlock and are invalid.

Examples

Stepwise Reducer functions are applied during pipeline evaluation after the Reducer stage has produced a candidate value. These functions do not return data or modify state. Instead, they evaluate the current snapshot and candidate value and explicitly decide how the pipeline should proceed.

Example 8: Policy-Based Pipeline Control

{{`employeeCell.withStepwiseReducer({
  stepwiseCallback: (current, candidate, decisions) => {

    // Clear state entirely if the candidate violates a hard policy
    if (candidate.some(e => e.status === 'Suspended')) {
      decisions.clear();
      return;
    }

    // Suppress the update if it fails a soft policy check
    if (candidate.length === 0) {
      decisions.block();
      return;
    }

    // Otherwise, allow the pipeline to proceed normally
    decisions.continue();
  }
}).initialize();

/*
Decision outcomes:
- Suspended employee detected → state cleared
- Empty candidate list       → update suppressed
- Valid candidate            → pipeline continues
*/`}}

This example demonstrates all three Stepwise Reducer outcomes:

  • continue() — admits the candidate value into downstream pipeline stages
  • block() — suppresses the update without altering existing state
  • clear() — resets state by explicitly clearing the current value

Stepwise Reducer functions must always issue exactly one decision. Failing to do so results in invalid pipeline behavior and will be rejected by the FeatureCell.

Stepwise Reducer Anti-Pattern Examples

The following examples demonstrate invalid Stepwise Reducer function behavior. These patterns violate the Stepwise Reducer contract by either failing to emit a decision or by depending on external mutable state. Such violations introduce nondeterminism or policy deadlocks and are detected and rejected by the FeatureCell to preserve deterministic pipeline control.

Example 9: Invalid — Missing Decision (Policy Deadlock)

{{`employeeCell.withStepwiseReducer({
  stepwiseCallback: (current, candidate, decisions) => {
    if (candidate.length > 5) {
      // ❌ forgot to call decisions.continue()
      return;
    }
  }
}).initialize();

// ❌ Vault error: Stepwise Reducer function did not emit a decision.
// This creates a policy deadlock and prevents the FeatureCell from processing further updates.`}}

Example 10: Invalid — External Mutable State

{{`let threshold = 5;

employeeCell.withStepwiseReducer({
  stepwiseCallback: (current, candidate, decisions) => {
    if (candidate.length > threshold) {
      decisions.continue();
    } else {
      decisions.block();
    }
  }
}).initialize();

// ❌ Vault error: Stepwise Reducer function depends on external mutable state`}}
